papers.what_it_is: A theory paper from D-Wave that compares incoherent quantum tunneling with the escape rate of quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) using perturbation theory, and argues QMC escape scales worse than tunneling when a problem has many homotopy-inequivalent tunneling paths, as frustrated problems can.

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier work (Isakov et al. and Jiang et al.) showed analytically, in the large spin limit with the WKB approximation, for a fully connected uniform ferromagnet at low temperature, that the QMC escape rate scales like the incoherent tunneling rate, both proportional to the square of the multi-qubit tunneling amplitude g.
quotes: It was shown analytically that, in the large spin limit using WKB approximation, for a fully-connected ferromagnet with uniform coupling, and when the temperature is low
ΓQMC ∝ g2 ∝ Γtunl,
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that the incoherent tunneling rate is proportional to the square of the multi-qubit tunneling amplitude g divided by W, the multi-qubit dephasing rate due to noise.
quotes: the rate of incoherent tunneling, Γtunl, is proportional to the square of the multi-qubit tunneling amplitude, g, between the
where W is the multi-qubit dephasing rate due to noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: A relation the paper cites to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they consider only QMC algorithms with local updates, such as path integral QMC with the standard updates used for spin-glass simulations, and that such algorithms work only when there is no sign problem, which requires a stoquastic Hamiltonian (no positive off-diagonal elements).
quotes: In this paper, we only consider QMC algorithms with local updates such as path integral QMC with standard updates used for spin-glass simulations [10].
These algorithms can work as long as there is no sign problem, which requires the Hamiltonian be stoquastic [11]
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of the algorithms it studies in Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state that QMC can be considered a simulation of quantum annealing only if its performance is both statistically and dynamically similar to that of a quantum annealer, and they do not consider open boundary QMC or diffusion Monte Carlo as viable simulations of quantum annealing because those cannot give correct equilibrium statistics by construction.
quotes: We emphasize that QMC can be considered a simulation of QA only if its performance is both statistically and dynamically similar to that of a quantum annealer.
we do not consider open boundary QMC [1] or diﬀusion Monte Carlo [21] as viable simulations of QA, because they cannot give correct equilibrium statistics by construction [32].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own criterion for what counts as a QMC simulation of QA.

assertions.value: The authors state that they show incoherent tunneling and QMC escape do not scale the same way when there are multiple homotopy-inequivalent paths for tunneling, and that frustration can generate an exponential number of tunneling paths, which under certain conditions can lead to an exponential advantage for incoherent tunneling over classical QMC escape.
quotes: We show that the two do not scale the same way when there are multiple homotopy-inequivalent paths for tunneling.

We demonstrate through examples that frustration can generate an exponential number of tunneling paths, which under certain conditions can lead to an exponential advantage for incoherent tunneling over classical QMC escape.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract's summary of the paper's main claim; the supporting derivation and numerics are entered separately.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study only incoherent tunneling and QMC escape at one particular point of the anneal, in the regime where the tunneling amplitude is small (the point is close to the end of the anneal), and that the classical part of the Hamiltonian forms a double-well potential with two identical minima.
quotes: Here, we only focus on incoherent tunneling and QMC escape at a particular point, s∗,
forms a double-well potential with two minima
We assume that the two potential wells are identical
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section II A.

assertions.value: The authors assume the temperature T is larger than the gap 2g between the two lowest levels (g being the multi-qubit tunneling amplitude) but much smaller than the gap to the excited states, so that only the two lowest energy levels are populated in thermal equilibrium; thermally assisted tunneling is beyond the scope of the paper.
quotes: We will also assume that the temperature T is larger than the gap 2g but much smaller than δE, so that only the two lowest energy levels are populated in thermal equilibrium.
but this is beyond the scope of this paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own temperature regime and scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the perturbation flips one qubit per application, the lowest order that can couple the two minima equals their Hamming distance L, and that to lowest order in the single-qubit amplitude Delta the tunneling amplitude g is a sum over all paths of L bit flips connecting the two minima, with intermediate energies above E0, of Delta to the power L divided by the product of the intermediate energy differences.
quotes: If the Hamming distance between the two wells is L, then the lowest order perturbation that can generate oﬀ-diagonal terms between the minima is L.
The tunneling amplitude to the lowest order in ∆ is given by [25]
where we have summed over all paths PL that connect |u to |d through L bit-ﬂips with intermediate energies satisfying El > E0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with a citation to prior work (reference 25); the statement is quoted but the equation text is garbled in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The formula itself (Eq. 7) is an equation whose symbols the text layer scatters; the value restates it in words from the PDF page.

assertions.value: The authors state that QMC rests on the observation that the equilibrium statistics of a D-dimensional stoquastic quantum Hamiltonian equal those of a (D+1)-dimensional classical Hamiltonian with appropriately chosen parameters, where the extra dimension (imaginary time) has a periodic boundary condition.
assertions.anchor: Section III, p.3; Appendix A, p.9
quotes: Quantum Monte Carlo simulation is based on the observation that equilibrium statistics of a D-dimensional (stoquastic) quantum Hamiltonian are equivalent to those of a (D+1)-dimensional classical Hamiltonian with appropriately chosen parameters
The additional dimension, sometimes called imaginary time, has a periodic boundary condition.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states, as the basis of its method, the standard QMC mapping and derives it in Appendix A.

assertions.value: The authors derive that, under the condition that 2g is much smaller than T which is much smaller than the gap to excited states, the ratio of the boundary partition function ZB (the loops making a single round trip between the two minima) to the local partition function of a minimum equals beta squared times g squared, where beta is the inverse temperature; they call this the central result of the paper.
quotes: Under the condition 2g T δE, we can write
Equations (11) and (12) are the central results of this paper, which lie at the heart of relation (2) observed in Refs. [1, 2].
ZB = β2g2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived to lowest order in Section III A, Eq. (13), under the quoted temperature condition.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the much-less-than signs in the condition 2g << T << delta E; the PDF page shows them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the relations for the local and boundary partition functions hold to all orders of perturbation theory (shown in Appendix C), assuming at low temperature that terms involving derivatives of the effective-Hamiltonian functions are negligible, but they note that evaluating the full series explicitly seems out of reach.
assertions.anchor: Section III A, p.4; Appendix C, pp.10-11
quotes: We show in Appendix C that (11) and (12) hold to all orders of perturbation theory.
Since evaluating (C5) explicitely seems to be out of reach, we pursue a diﬀerent approach.
At low temperature βbb β2a b2 and we obtain
assertions.certainty_reason: The Appendix C argument neglects derivative terms under a low-temperature assumption rather than evaluating them, so the all-orders claim is argued, not fully proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that, if the escape rate is much smaller than the equilibration rate within the well holding the initial minimum, local equilibrium statistics can determine the escape rate, and that this assumption is met for QMC in the regime 2g much smaller than T much smaller than the gap to excited states; they then expect the QMC escape rate to be proportional to the ratio of the barrier partition function to the local partition function of the minimum.
quotes: if the escape rate is much smaller than the equilibration rate within the well that contains the initial local minimum, the local equilibrium statistics can determine the escape rate.
This assumption is met for QMC in the regime 2g T δE.
we expect the escape rate ΓQMC to be proportional to the ratio of the total equilibrium probability of the loops L in a small neighborhood of the saddle point (barrier) S
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors expect this proportionality, drawing on multidimensional Kramers theory, rather than prove it.

assertions.value: The authors derive that with only one dominant tunneling path the barrier partition function equals the boundary partition function ZB, so the QMC escape rate is proportional to beta squared g squared, confirming the earlier relation that QMC escape rate and incoherent tunneling rate scale the same way.
quotes: The sum over conﬁgurations in the neighborhood of C is precisely ZB and we have ZB = Zbarrier.
conﬁrming the relation (2), which was observed by [1].
assertions.certainty_reason: A perturbative argument that rests on the stated expected proportionality of escape rate to barrier partition function; the conditions are only partly quoted.

assertions.value: The authors derive that with two equivalent tunneling paths, where a loop stretching along both paths must pass through high-energy states and that channel is suppressed, the QMC escape rate is dominated by the two single-path channels and is half the single-path value, giving a factor of 2 quantum advantage for incoherent tunneling over QMC.
quotes: When the loop stretches along both paths, as in Fig. 3(b), it cannot stay within the low-energy states (blue lines) and has to pass through high-energy states during the escape process, as depicted in B and D.
There is a factor of 2 quantum advantage for incoherent
assertions.certainty_reason: A perturbative, schematic argument whose inter-path suppression holds only under the energy-gap and entropy condition entered separately.

assertions.value: The authors state that inter-path tunneling is suppressed, and the factor-of-two advantage holds, only if the energy gap between the low-energy states and the excited states is large enough to offset the entropy difference; because the number of paths typically grows with system size the gap has to grow with size, and when the condition is violated the advantage disappears and QMC escape follows the single-path scaling.
quotes: In order for this relation to hold, the energy gap between the low-energy states and the excited states has to be large enough to oﬀset the entropy diﬀerence between the two.
As the system size increases, one has to increase the energy gap because the number of paths typically grows with the system size.
When (20) is violated, inter-path tunneling will not be suppressed anymore
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the condition under which its factor-of-two result holds.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated limit attaches to a derived (theoretical) result, which is why the result type is theoretical rather than measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of constructive interference between the paths, incoherent tunneling scales as the square of the number of homotopy-inequivalent paths whereas QMC escape scales linearly with that number, as long as the inter-path escape channels are forbidden, so that the QMC escape rate is proportional to the tunneling rate divided by the number of paths.
quotes: Because of constructive interference between the paths, quantum incoherent tunneling scales as Np2aths, whereas QMC escape scales as Npaths, as long as the inter-path escape channels are forbidden.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling argument extended from the two-path case, conditional on the inter-path channels being forbidden.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer printed the exponent flat (Np2aths for N_paths squared).

assertions.value: The authors state that for the uniform fully connected ferromagnet all tunneling paths are homotopy equivalent, so path multiplicity creates no topological obstruction and the QMC escape rate and tunneling rate scale the same way, in agreement with (and more general than) the result of Isakov et al.
quotes: In other words, all tunneling paths are homotopy equivalent, i.e., Npaths = 1.
The multiplicity of the paths therefore does not lead to topological obstructions and we obtain (2), in agreement with (although more general than) the result obtained in Ref. [1].
assertions.certainty_reason: A theoretical argument for one example, not an experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a ring of qubits with ferromagnetic couplers and one weaker antiferromagnetic coupler, in the limit where the frustration energy epsilon is much smaller than J, there are two dominant tunneling paths between the two classical ground states, one flipping the qubits in order 1 to N and the other in reverse order.
quotes: there are two dominant tunneling paths, with energy barrier El−E0 = 2
In path 1 the qubits are ﬂipped in the order 1, 2, . . . , N , while in path 2 the qubits are ﬂipped in the reverse order.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theoretical example whose symbols (epsilon, much-less-than) the text layer partly drops.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the epsilon symbol in the barrier 2 epsilon; the PDF page shows it.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the frustrated ring all states on the two tunneling paths have 1 violated coupling while all other states have at least 3 violated couplings, so that when J is much larger than epsilon the inter-path loops are energetically suppressed, leading to topological obstructions and quantum advantage.
quotes: All the states involved in these two tunneling paths have 1 violated coupling while all other states outside this subspace have at least 3 violated couplings.
then the inter-path loops are energetically suppressed, leading to topological obstructions and quantum advantage (19).
assertions.certainty_reason: A theoretical argument for one example.

assertions.value: The authors state that although the energy gap to states outside the two paths does not change with ring size, the entropy of the inter-path loops increases with N, so at very large sizes the inter-path loops may escape and reduce the factor of one half unless J divided by epsilon is increased with N.
quotes: At very large sizes the inter-path loops may ﬁnd a chance to escape due to the large entropy and therefore reduce the factor of 1/2, unless J/ is increased with N .
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size limit of its two-path advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the shamrock graph of K frustrated rings sharing a common node there are two to the power K tunneling paths, and that, assuming all inter-path QMC escape channels are topologically forbidden, the QMC escape rate is proportional to the tunneling rate divided by two to the power K, an exponential advantage of incoherent tunneling over QMC escape.
quotes: the total number of paths will be 2K. Assuming that all the inter-path QMC escape channels are topologically forbidden, we obtain
This is an exponential advantage of incoherent tunneling over QMC escape.
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling argument conditional on the topological-obstruction assumption, supported by the numerical test entered separately.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer printed the exponent flat (2K for 2 to the power K).

assertions.value: The authors report that they ran continuous-time QMC simulations starting from the all-up state with parameters Delta = A = 0.5, B = 1, beta = 20, J = 6 and epsilon = 0.2, defining the escape time as the mean first passage time, the minimal time for the QMC world-line to have some minimal support (5% in their calculations) on the target state, with error bars showing statistical error over 1000 independent runs.
assertions.anchor: Section IV C, p.7; Figure 6 caption, p.8
quotes: Similar to Ref. [1], we deﬁne escape time as mean ﬁrst passage time, i.e. minimal time it takes QMC world-line to have some minimal (5% in our
The simulation parameters are: ∆ = A = 0.5, B = 1, β = 20, J = 6, and = 0.2.
The error bars represent statistical error for 1000 independent simulation runs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the setup of its own numerical test.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the epsilon symbol before the 0.2; the PDF page shows it.

assertions.value: The authors report, for shamrock graphs with K = 1 to 7 rings (N = 3 to 15 qubits), that both the QMC escape time and 1/g squared scale exponentially with N but QMC scales worse, and that the curve two to the power K divided by g squared fits the QMC sweeps very well, which they say confirms the exponential-advantage relation; g is the minimum gap found by exact diagonalization.
quotes: Figure 6 shows the results of numerical calculations for shamrock graphs of Fig. 5 with K = 1 to 7 rings (N = 3 to 15 qubits).
Both QMC escape time and 1/g2 scale exponentially with N , but QMC scales worse.
which ﬁts very well with the QMC sweeps conﬁrming (24).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the chosen simulation parameters the condition Delta < 2 epsilon needed for the perturbation expansion is violated, yet the exponential superiority predicted for the shamrock still holds in the numerical results.
assertions.anchor: Figure 6 caption, p.8; Section IV C, p.8
quotes: Notice that the condition ∆ < 2 necessary for perturbation expansion is violated.
Notice that with the parameters chosen, ∆ > 2 and therefore perturbation theory does not hold while the exponential superiority predicted in (24) remains valid.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the epsilon symbols; the PDF page shows Delta < 2 epsilon.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 6: the normalized escape time of the QMC sweeps rises from about 1 at N = 3 to about 3 million at N = 15, lying on the dashed line two to the power K divided by g squared, while the solid 1/g squared line rises more slowly, to about 60 thousand at N = 15; both are straight lines on the log axis.
quotes: (N = 3 to 15 qubits)
Normalized escape time as a function of the number of qubits for the shamrock problems in Fig. 5.
The agreement between the symbols and the blue dashed line conﬁrms (24).
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as the shamrock graphs are scaled to larger sizes, the entropy of the inter-path loops must be watched, and that to keep the exponential advantage one may need to increase J divided by epsilon linearly with N.
quotes: Once again, one should be careful about the entropy of the inter-path loops as the shamrock graphs are scaled to larger sizes.
to keep the above exponential advantage one may need to increase J/ linearly with N .
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the size limit on its shamrock result.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that constructive interference, the only kind possible for stoquastic Hamiltonians, can give incoherent tunneling an advantage over QMC in the presence of topological obstructions, that the advantage can increase linearly with the number of tunneling paths, and that frustration can produce multiple tunneling paths and so a quantum advantage.
quotes: Constructive interference, which is the only one possible for stoquastic Hamiltonians, can lead to quantum advantage for incoherent tunneling in the presence of topological obstructions.
The advantage can linearly increase with the number of tunneling paths.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from their derivations and one numerical example.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that in frustrated systems the number of tunneling paths can increase exponentially with the number of qubits that tunnel together, which can lead to an exponential quantum advantage as long as the topological obstructions remain effective, which requires careful examination of the entropy of the excited states involved.
quotes: We have shown through examples that in frustrated systems the number of tunneling paths can increase exponentially with the number of qubits that tunnel together.
This can lead to an exponential quantum advantage as long as the topological obstructions remain eﬀective
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, conditional on the topological obstructions staying effective.

assertions.value: The authors state that although perturbation expansion was used in the main derivations, the results hold beyond perturbation theory, which they demonstrate in a numerical example and with a derivation in Appendix C.
quotes: While perturbation expansion was used in the main derivations of our work, the results hold beyond perturbation theory.
We have demonstrated this in a numerical example and give a derivation in Appendix C beyond perturbation theory.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim supported by one numerical example and an approximate derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the incoherent tunneling rate relation does not capture all the physics of incoherent tunneling, that resonant tunneling and polaron effects, which matter in the quantum tunneling analysis, are not captured by QMC, and that they therefore expect an additional advantage of order the square root of N beyond what is shown in Figure 6.
quotes: does not capture all the physics of incoherent tunneling.
resonant tunneling [19, 20, 22] and polaron eﬀects [20], which are important in the quantum tunneling analysis, are not captured by QMC
quantum advantage is expected beyond what is shown in Fig. 6.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states what its model of incoherent tunneling leaves out.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer dropped the square-root sign before N; the PDF page shows an additional sqrt(N) advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that incoherent tunneling is not the main quantum resource for quantum annealing, that the resource is the ability to form large-scale superposition and entanglement, and that the exponential speedup of quantum annealing shown by Somma et al. would disappear if the algorithm relied merely on incoherent tunneling events.
quotes: Finally, we should emphasize that incoherent tunneling is not the main quantum resource for QA.
Indeed, the exponential speedup of QA vs classical algorithms, demostrated by Somma et al. [23], would disappear if the algorithm relys merely on incoherent tunneling events.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement, partly citing another result, without evidence in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that reproducing the interference effects by QMC requires overcoming topological obstructions, and that this is closely related to the topological obstructions for QMC discussed by Hastings and Freedman.
quotes: However, as we shall show, reproduction of the interference eﬀects by QMC requires overcoming topological obstructions.
This is closely related to the topological obstructions for QMC discussed by Hastings and Freedman [24].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement tied to cited work.

papers.what_it_is: A survey and position paper that proposes a definition of explainable AI built around the audience, taxonomies of transparent and post-hoc explainability methods for machine learning and deep learning (about 400 contributions), challenges, and the concept of Responsible AI.

assertions.value: The authors define an explainable Artificial Intelligence, given an audience, as one that produces details or reasons to make its functioning clear or easy to understand, and present this as the first contribution of the overview.

This deﬁnition is posed here as a ﬁrst contribution of the present overview

quotes: Therefore, the deﬁnition must be rephrased to reﬂect explicitly the dependence of the explainability of the model on the audience.

contrast, explainability can be viewed as an active characteristic of a model, denoting any action or procedure taken by a model with the intent of clarifying or detailing its internal functions.

assertions.value: The authors state that slow two-level-system diffusion can alter the performance of qubits over hours or days, that it is likely the H10 data set was collected when the best performing qubits had worse coupling to an itinerant TLS than when the H12 data set was collected, and that they show all results without cherry picking or rerunning less performant curves.

We believe that by showing all of these results without cherry picking and rerunning less performant curves, we give a more accurate representation of the average performance of the device.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a caveat on the comparability of its own data sets.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table II that the average post-selection shot ratio, the fraction of the 250,000 circuit repetitions kept, is 0.764(7) for H6, 0.66(1) for H8, 0.56(1) for H10, 0.46(2) for H12 and 0.44(1) for diazene, decreasing with system size and almost perfectly tracking a joint readout fidelity of 95%.

assertions.value: The authors state that the significant improvement in readout scatter from post-selection is a fundamental driver in the success of the experiment, due to the sensitivity of quantum chemistry energies to electron number, and that they believe the discrepancy between the two 10-qubit experiments stems from the diazene circuits having more idle moments where qubits can decay.
quotes: The signiﬁcant improvement in readout scatter from post-selection is a fundamental driver in the success of this experiment due to the sensitivity of quantum chemistry energies to electron number.

We believe the discrepancy between the two 10-qubit experiments (H10 and diazene experiments) stems from the fact that the diazene circuits have more idle circuit moments where the qubits are free to decay.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation stated as belief.

assertions.value: The authors state that the correlation between fidelity and absolute energy error suggests that fidelity can be used as an optimization target for this system, a useful property when considering basis rotation states as targets for benchmarks and tune-up protocols.
quotes: The correlation in the ﬁdelity and absolute energy error suggests that ﬁdelity can be used as an optimization target for this system.
This is a useful property when considering basis rotation states as targets for benchmarks and tune-up protocols.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author suggestion from the observed correlation.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate H6 natural occupation numbers; for the first listed bond distance the raw values are 0.0024, 0.0181, 0.0338, 0.8738, 0.9109 and 0.9402, and after post-selection they are -0.0006, 0.0113, 0.0271, 0.9768, 0.9861 and 0.9993, moving the occupied values toward one and the virtual values toward zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental study.
assertions.reader_inference: Tables III to X list natural occupation numbers for the other chains; the pattern is the same: post-selection moves the large values from about 0.8 to 0.9 to about 0.93 to 1.0 and keeps small values near 0, with some post-selected values slightly above 1 or below 0.
